elements.content: Communication Goal: I can greet people, introduce myself, spell my name, and share contact details.

Lesson overview:
- Level: A0 General English
- Unit: Unit 1. Hello there!
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: Hello, friend!
- Materials: Whiteboard, name cards, alphabet chart, audio script, COSYmanuals 'to be' and 'pronouns' pages.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• greet people politely in English
• spell my name and share my email and phone number
• use survival phrases to keep a conversation going
Recycling & Course Continuity:

Prior learning: Recycles greetings and names from the first lesson.

Next lesson: Lesson 2 recycles introductions and adds jobs with a/an.
Quick retrieval task: which words or phrases do you remember?
Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (15 items):

hello — a greeting when you meet someone. Example: Hello, my name is Alex.
hi — an informal greeting. Example: Hi, how are you?
goodbye — a word you say when you leave. Example: Goodbye, see you tomorrow.
name — the word people use to call you. Example: My name is Sara.
spell — to say the letters of a word. Example: Can you spell your name, please?
student — a person who studies. Example: I am a student.
teacher — a person who helps students learn. Example: She is my English teacher.
friend — a person you like and know well. Example: Tom is my best friend.
alphabet — the letters A to Z. Example: The English alphabet has 26 letters.
email — an electronic address for messages. Example: My email is alex at school dot com.
phone — a device for calls and messages. Example: My phone number is 078-452-9103.
number — a set of digits used to identify something. Example: What is your phone number?
at — the symbol @ in an email address. Example: Write 'alex at school dot com'.
dot — the symbol . in an email address. Example: It is alex dot brown at mail dot com.
hyphen — the short line - in a word or number. Example: My email has a hyphen in it.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• Hello, my name is... (introducing yourself)
• Nice to meet you. (polite response when you meet someone)
• How are you? I'm fine, thanks. (greeting and answer)
• Can you spell your name, please? (asking for spelling)
• My email is ... at ... dot com. (sharing an email address)
• Sorry, can you repeat that? (asking someone to say it again)
• What does ... mean? (asking for meaning)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'a greeting when you meet someone'?
Which word means 'an informal greeting'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.

goodbye /ɡʊdˈbaɪ/ — stress the second syllable

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use 'be' to say who someone is, how they feel, and where they are from.

Form:
The verb 'to be': I am / You are / He, she, it is / We are / They are. Negative: I'm not, isn't, aren't. Question: Am I...? Are you...? Is he...?

Examples:
• I am a student.
• She is from Spain.
• We are happy today.
• They are not teachers.
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
My name ___ Alex.
They ___ from Italy.
I ___ tired today.
She ___ not a teacher.
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I am ... (a student / happy / from Egypt).
• She is ... (a teacher / tired / from Spain).
• They are ... (students / at home / happy).
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• Are you a student? — Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
• Is she from France? — Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
• Are they happy? — Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write two true sentences with 'I am...' and 'I am not...'.
• Introduce two people in the class with 'He/She is...'.
Reading: Hello, friend!

Hello! My name is Alex. I am a student. My email is alex at school dot com. My phone number is 078-452-9103. This is my friend Maria. She is a student too. Our teacher is Mr Brown. He is very nice. Sorry, can you repeat that? Yes, of course. What does 'email' mean? It is an electronic address. Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
What is Alex's email?
What is Alex's phone number?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Hello! My name is Alex.
B: Hi, Alex. I'm Maria.
A: Nice to meet you, Maria. Can you spell your name?
B: Yes, M-A-R-I-A.
A: And what is your email?
B: It's maria at school dot com.
A: Sorry, can you repeat that?
B: Maria at school dot com. M-A-R-I-A at school dot com.
How does Maria spell her name?
What is Maria's email?
Speaking task: Introduce yourself to three classmates. Spell your name and share your email or phone number.

• What do you say when you meet someone new?
• How do you spell your name?
• How do you say an email address in English?
• What do you say when you don't understand?
• Which survival phrase is most useful for you?
Role-play: You are at a workshop check-in. Give your name, spell it, share your email, and ask the staff member to repeat one detail.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write a contact card with your name, job or studies, email, phone number, and one survival phrase.
Model: Hi, I'm ... I'm a ... My email is ... at ... dot com. My phone number is ... Sorry, can you repeat that?
